Solution 3 is the closest, but its answer of 10 is wrong. It omits 7, which belongs to $P$.

**Checking $A_5$:** Its non-linear degrees are 3, 3, 4, 5, and each has exactly one distinct prime divisor. So $A_5 \in \mathcal{G}$ and $\{2,3,5\} \subseteq P$. Solution 2's claim that $A_5$'s non-linear degrees are only 3 and 4 is wrong, and it omits 5.

**Checking $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$:** Its character degrees are $1, 7, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9$ (the squares sum to $504 = |G|$). Every non-linear degree (7, 8, 9) has exactly one distinct prime divisor. So $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8) \in \mathcal{G}$, which puts $7 \in P$. Hence $P \supseteq \{2,3,5,7\}$, and the sum is at least 17, so 10 cannot be correct.

**Solution 1** claims $P$ is all primes and the sum is infinite. This is unsupported, and the argument it gives is internally inconsistent.

I did not complete a classification of $\mathcal{G}$, so I cannot state the exact value of the sum. What the checks above do establish is that none of the three proposed answers (infinity, 5, or 10) can be correct.

CHOICE: NONE
